nodes.label: net8.0 as pinned target framework
nodes.rationale: Chosen because builds.dotnet.microsoft.com is blocked by the proxy (HTTP 403), so dotnet-install.sh cannot fetch .NET 9/10; Ubuntu's archive carries dotnet-sdk-8.0. .NET 8 is also the most widely deployed enterprise LTS, matching interview reality. Accepted cost: .NET 8 leaves support before .NET 10, and roll-forward can confuse readers on newer SDKs.

nodes.label: System.Threading.Lock (.NET 9+)
nodes.rationale: A dedicated lock type replacing lock-on-object, avoiding the classic mistake of locking on something publicly reachable like `this` or a string. Cannot be demonstrated in running code here; covered as text in lesson 02 instead.

nodes.label: Multi-targeting net8.0;net10.0 (rejected)
nodes.rationale: Rejected: doubles build and test time and forces #if NET10_0_OR_GREATER branches through teaching code to demonstrate one keyword. Better described in a lesson than built into the project structure.

nodes.label: Directory.Build.props central pinning
nodes.rationale: TargetFramework pinned once for all five projects so the eventual upgrade is a one-line change plus a package bump.

nodes.label: CS1705 assembly-version build break
nodes.rationale: Package versions must stay on a mutually consistent 8.0.x line (EF Core 8.0.11, Npgsql 8.0.11); mixing 8.0.11 and 8.0.13 produced CS1705 once during setup.

nodes.label: ADR-0004 Hybrid persistence: in-memory and PostgreSQL
Hybrid storage split (group A in-memory, group B PostgreSQL)
nodes.rationale: Postgres everywhere would smother the first lesson behind four EF concepts (change tracker, unit of work, when SaveChanges emits SQL, changed-column UPDATE) and make the naive race harder to reproduce. In-memory everywhere would make the optimistic/pessimistic slices lies — DbUpdateConcurrencyException never raised, SELECT FOR UPDATE a comment. Accepted cost: two persistence models to hold in your head and non-zero setup.

nodes.label: InMemoryAccountStore (singleton, deliberately unsafe)
nodes.rationale: Registered as a singleton because shared mutable process state is the precondition for the race; scoping it would quietly delete the bug. Duplicates the database's Version and a TryWrite compare-and-swap on purpose, to show optimistic concurrency is a pattern rather than an EF feature. Process-local, so it misbehaves under multiple replicas — which is the point of ADR-0014.

nodes.label: EF Core in-memory provider (rejected)
nodes.rationale: Not a shortcut: it implements neither concurrency tokens nor row locking, so tests would pass against a system that is still broken.

nodes.label: static ConcurrentDictionary as source of truth (trap)
nodes.rationale: Works perfectly on one instance and corrupts silently on two — the failure mode this repo demonstrates on purpose. Legitimate in-memory state is caches you can afford to lose, per-request scoped state, and single-writer designs.

nodes.label: PostgreSQL 16
nodes.rationale: Free, no licence acceptance, small footprint, real row-level locking, xmin as a schema-free concurrency token, and advisory locks for distributed locking with no extra infrastructure. Decisive here: no Docker daemon, while PostgreSQL 16 was already installed and startable natively.

nodes.label: xmin system column as concurrency token
nodes.rationale: Mapped as Version with type xid; costs nothing in schema because pg_attribute.attnum = -2 makes Npgsql's migration generator emit no DDL. Postgres-specific: porting to SQL Server means a byte[] RowVersion with [Timestamp].

nodes.label: SELECT … FOR UPDATE row locking
nodes.rationale: Standard SQL, and it ports to SQL Server as WITH (UPDLOCK, ROWLOCK).

nodes.label: SQLite (rejected on capability)
nodes.rationale: Locking is file/database-level, not row-level — writers serialise across the whole database, so a pessimistic lock on one account is indistinguishable from a lock on every account. No SELECT FOR UPDATE, no meaningful deadlock scenario; a test proving pessimistic locking works would pass for the wrong reason.

nodes.label: SQL Server (rejected on friction)
nodes.rationale: The close call, lost on friction rather than merit: large image, EULA acceptance, more memory than a lab container has, and no Docker daemon in this environment. Its rowversion token is the more familiar one to .NET developers, which ADR-0006 covers explicitly.

nodes.label: ADR-0007 Optimistic by default, pessimistic by exception
Optimistic concurrency as the default
nodes.rationale: Measured on identical input (5 actors, 100 each, 100 balance, forced race): optimistic 9 attempts / 4 conflicts / 0.0 ms waiting vs pessimistic 5 attempts / 0 conflicts / 244.1 ms waiting. Optimistic holds no locks across requests so it scales horizontally. Accepted costs: retry logic in every write path, a failure mode that only appears under load, and starvation because retries have no queue.

nodes.label: Pessimistic used deliberately for named reasons
nodes.rationale: Reserved for hot rows, work expensive to redo, and first-come-first-served business rules. Pessimistic-by-default was rejected because it couples correctness to holding a resource: every waiter occupies a connection, deadlock becomes a standing risk on multi-entity operations, and it is incompatible with user think time.

nodes.label: OptimisticWithdrawHandler.MaxAttempts = 5
nodes.rationale: Bounded retry: exhausting attempts returns a refusal rather than looping, because unbounded retry under contention is a livelock — everything busy, nothing progressing — and harder to diagnose than a deadlock since nothing looks stuck.

nodes.label: Only the first attempt joins the interleaving barrier
nodes.rationale: Retries must not re-join, because by then some actors have finished and would never arrive, so the barrier would stall the rest until its timeout.

nodes.label: Conflict rate as the deciding variable
nodes.rationale: Rough thresholds: under ~1% of writes conflicting, optimistic is comfortable; over ~10% you do more work retrying than a lock would cost. The better answer is to ask whether the hot row can be removed — shard the counter, queue the writes, event-source it.

nodes.label: Jittered exponential backoff (named, not implemented)
nodes.rationale: Production advice this repo names but does not implement: retrying immediately means the same actors collide again in the same order.

nodes.label: ADR-0008 A test-controlled interleaving seam in production code
IInterleaveGate injected seam
nodes.rationale: The most arguable decision in the repo. Handlers call gate.ReachAsync at one named checkpoint; a no-op in production, a barrier when a run opts into a forced race. Defensible because forceRace is a product feature (a real runtime caller, not test-only) and because without it the project's central claim — deterministic, reproducible races — is false. In a real banking service it should be compiled out behind #if DEBUG, a build-stripped feature flag, or InternalsVisibleTo.

nodes.label: LabInterleaveGate
nodes.rationale: Returns Task.CompletedTask after a single ConcurrentDictionary lookup unless a run registered itself as a forced race; the gate caps forcing at 5 seconds so a mis-placed checkpoint cannot hang forever.

nodes.label: InterleaveCheckpoints (AfterRead / BeforeAcquire)
nodes.rationale: AfterRead for lock-free strategies, BeforeAcquire for locking ones. Proven during development: the locking handler originally gated inside its critical section, so the lock holder waited at a barrier for actors who could not enter until it released — a real deadlock. Checkpoint choice is part of writing a slice, not an afterthought.

nodes.label: AsyncBarrier
nodes.rationale: Exists because System.Threading.Barrier blocks its thread — using it would mean N thread-pool threads blocked waiting on each other, the very starvation bug lesson 09 is about. The lab would cause the problem it teaches.

nodes.label: Thread.Sleep/Task.Delay in the handler (rejected)
nodes.rationale: The worst option and the most commonly reached for: makes the race likelier but never certain, slows every run including production, and the delay is a magic number simultaneously too short on loaded CI and too long everywhere else.

nodes.label: Statistical brute force (rejected)
nodes.rationale: Slow and still non-deterministic; it inverts the assertion so a test cannot distinguish a lost update from an unrelated fault, and it cannot express specific interleavings such as 'all five actors read before any writes'.

nodes.label: Microsoft Coyote / CHESS deterministic schedulers
nodes.rationale: Systematically explore interleavings rather than sampling them; naming Coyote signals awareness that a hand-rolled barrier is the small version of a solved problem class.

nodes.label: ADR-0009 SignalR for the live timeline
SignalR live contention feed
nodes.rationale: Chosen over SSE because SignalR's group model gives per-run fan-out for free and because SignalR is itself a standard .NET interview topic. Polling the finished run is kept as a fallback and for replay, but loses the property that matters: seeing events arrive while contention is happening.

nodes.label: ContentionHub (WatchRun / StopWatchingRun)
nodes.rationale: Clients join group run-{id}. Groups live in the process, so with multiple replicas a client on instance 2 misses events published on instance 1 — the same bug as the in-process lock, in a different costume.

nodes.label: ContentionBroadcaster BackgroundService
nodes.rationale: Drains the recorder's channel so a slow or broken client can never slow down a bank withdrawal; broadcast failures are logged and swallowed. Pushing inline from Record() would put a network call inside the critical section being measured.

nodes.label: Server-Sent Events (rejected, close call)
nodes.rationale: Arguably the better engineering choice in isolation — the feed is one-directional and EventSource needs no client dependency — but it would need hand-rolled per-run subscriber bookkeeping, and SignalR is the thing interviews ask about.

nodes.label: Redis backplane and sticky sessions
nodes.rationale: Required once there is more than one replica, because SignalR groups are per-process and WebSocket connections are long-lived so the load balancer must pin a client to one instance.

nodes.label: ADR-0010 Three performance tools, three different jobs
BenchmarkDotNet (micro, in-process)
nodes.rationale: Handles JIT warmup, tiered compilation, outlier detection, statistical significance, memory diagnostics and dead-code elimination — all of which hand-rolled Stopwatch code gets wrong below about a millisecond. Pointing it at an HTTP endpoint is a category error: no concurrency, no pooling, no contention.

nodes.label: In-repo load harness (tests/Bank.LoadTests)
nodes.rationale: A dependency-free replacement for NBomber: computes RPS and percentiles from a latency array and stops there. Accepted as worse than k6 or NBomber — no ramp-up profiles, no distributed generation, no polished reporting — and risks measuring itself, mitigated by keeping it simple and async and cross-checking against the k6 scripts.

nodes.label: k6 scripts (loadtests/k6)
nodes.rationale: Would have been the better macro tool, but its binary cannot be downloaded through this environment's proxy. Scripts are committed anyway because k6 is what most teams use and they run on a developer's own machine.

nodes.label: NBomber (rejected on licence)
nodes.rationale: The original plan, dropped after reading the licence: version 3.0 (effective September 2025) is a commercial subscription whose NuGet package sets requireLicenseAcceptance and ships a licence file instead of an SPDX expression — the same disqualifier applied to MediatR and FluentAssertions in ADR-0002.

nodes.label: Benchmarking vs load testing separation
nodes.rationale: Bank.Benchmarks never makes an HTTP call; Bank.LoadTests never calls a method directly. The separation is structural so the category error is hard to make by accident. Benchmarking finds slow code; load testing finds slow systems, and the bottleneck is usually a pool or a lock that no in-process benchmark can see — evidenced by sync-over-async, which benchmarks fine and starves the thread pool under load.

nodes.label: ADR-0011 Angular standalone components + signals, no NgRx
Standalone components with signals
nodes.rationale: The UI's whole state is the last run's result and an in-flight flag. Signals replace BehaviorSubjects without manual async pipes or subscription lifecycle. Accepted costs: no time-travel debugging, state does not survive navigation, and the approach would not scale to a large app. Routes lazy-load each page so the initial bundle stays around 85 kB gzipped.

nodes.label: NgRx (rejected)
nodes.rationale: Its benefits — shared state across distant components, time-travel debugging, disciplined mutation in a large team — do not apply to pages that share no state. The ceremony would work against the repo's purpose: a reader trying to understand a race condition should not first have to understand a reducer. A store is a coordination tool; adding one before you have a coordination problem is the same mistake as reaching for a lock you don't need.

nodes.label: ContentionHubService (degrades silently)
nodes.rationale: If the websocket never opens the page still works, because the run response carries the whole timeline. A demo that dies because a socket didn't connect is a bad demo.

nodes.label: UI holds no business logic
nodes.rationale: Every verdict — who won, who lost silently, whether money was conserved — is computed server-side by RunSummaryCalculator, because that logic is the subject being taught and it has tests. The UI cannot disagree with the tests because it computes nothing they cover. Animations are plain CSS, so @angular/animations is not a dependency and prefers-reduced-motion is one media query.

nodes.label: ADR-0012 PostgreSQL advisory locks for distributed locking
pg_advisory_lock as distributed lock
nodes.rationale: Mutual exclusion on an arbitrary 64-bit key in a database already running, so no new infrastructure. Session-scoped rather than transaction-scoped because the caller may not be in a transaction; releasing is therefore ours, but disposing the context closes the connection and Postgres releases every advisory lock it held, so the lock cannot leak. Measured cost: ~2.6 s total waiting for 5 contending actors versus ~8 ms on the in-process semaphore. Only earns its place when the thing serialised is not a single database row.

nodes.label: IAccountLock abstraction
nodes.rationale: Two implementations differing only in DI registration, so one line is the entire difference between code that scales and code that doesn't. WorksAcrossInstances is exposed on the interface and surfaced through /api/lab/strategies so the UI can label which strategies survive scale-out.

nodes.label: PostgresAdvisoryAccountLock
nodes.rationale: Opens a dedicated DbContext because a session-scoped advisory lock is tied to its connection — enough concurrent holders exhausts the pool, the same failure mode as long pessimistic transactions. The Guid key is hashed into 64 bits, so two accounts can collide and share a lock: unnecessary blocking, never incorrectness.

nodes.label: InProcessAccountLock
nodes.rationale: Correct on one instance and silently wrong on three — the cliffhanger lesson 02 ends on.

nodes.label: Redis / Redlock (rejected)
nodes.rationale: Faster and the obvious production choice where Redis already runs, but adding infrastructure to teach one concept makes a lesson people skip; and a single-node Redis lock is not safe under failover while Redlock's safety is actively disputed (Kleppmann), so teaching it as settled would be wrong.

nodes.label: Fencing token
nodes.rationale: The mitigation for a TTL-based lock expiring while the holder still believes it holds it (a long GC pause is enough): a monotonically increasing number the downstream resource checks. Not needed with a Postgres advisory lock, where the connection dropping releases the lock automatically — no TTL to tune, no orphan.

nodes.label: ADR-0013 Contention events in a bounded in-memory buffer
Bounded per-run event buffer (20,000 events, 50 runs)
nodes.rationale: Recording happens inside the code under observation, so the observer must not perturb what it observes, and it must never grow without bound — an unbounded buffer under load is just a slow memory leak. Accepted: events lost on restart, older runs 404, memory bounded but not small, and the buffer is process-local like SignalR groups.

nodes.label: Channel<ContentionEvent> producer/consumer split
nodes.rationale: Deliberately unbounded so TryWrite always succeeds and the producer can never block; bounding it would mean either blocking a withdrawal or dropping events, and for a lab 'never distort the measurement' beats 'never allocate'. Channel<T> is async-native where BlockingCollection blocks a thread-pool thread and an event handler runs on the caller's thread.

nodes.label: Record() hot path
nodes.rationale: An Interlocked.Increment, a queue enqueue and a non-blocking channel write — no locks, no I/O, no allocation beyond the event itself. Interlocked rather than lock because a counter needs atomicity, not mutual exclusion: cheaper, and it cannot deadlock.

nodes.label: LabRunStore / RunSummary retention
nodes.rationale: RunSummary is computed once at the end of a run and stored separately, so a verdict outlives the event eviction it was derived from.

nodes.label: Persisting events to PostgreSQL or a log sink (rejected)
nodes.rationale: Persisting puts a database round-trip inside the critical section of a benchmark about database contention — the recording contends with the thing recorded. Log sinks buffer and batch on their own schedule, so ordering and latency become the framework's business, unacceptable when the ordering is the data.

nodes.label: ADR-0014 Docker Compose replicas; Kubernetes deliberately excluded
Three-replica Compose demo behind nginx
nodes.rationale: The lesson is that process-local state does not survive multiple instances, and Compose shows it in about 30 seconds with a file anyone can read end to end. Accepted: Compose is not production (no rolling deploys, health routing, autoscaling or self-healing), and the demo has never been executed here — no Docker daemon, so the files are only `docker compose config`-validated.

nodes.label: Kubernetes (rejected)
nodes.rationale: Adds enormous operational surface and not one concurrency insight — manifests, a local cluster, an ingress controller and an image registry before the same demonstration. It would also mislead by implying scaling is a Kubernetes topic. Kubernetes is warranted for operational properties (rolling deploys, self-healing, autoscaling, service discovery), never to make code fast.

nodes.label: nginx round-robin (not sticky)
nodes.rationale: Breaks SignalR across replicas; documented rather than fixed with sticky sessions, because finding it yourself is more instructive than having it silently handled.

nodes.label: INSTANCE_ID per service
nodes.rationale: Injected per service and returned by /api/health and the scale endpoints, so you can see which replica served each request.

nodes.label: loadtests/k6/hot-account.js
nodes.rationale: The script that exposes the in-process lock, because it drives concurrent requests through nginx — the lab's own runner drives all actors from within one instance and therefore cannot show the failure.

nodes.label: ADR-0015 Local PostgreSQL + Respawn, not Testcontainers
Local PostgreSQL + Respawn test database
nodes.rationale: Chosen only because there is no /var/run/docker.sock in this build environment — the docker CLI and dockerd exist but there is no daemon to talk to. Accepted costs: an external prerequisite (dotnet test fails with a connection error, mitigated by BANKLAB_TEST_DB), possible state leaks between runs, version drift, and limited parallelism against one shared database.

nodes.label: Testcontainers (rejected on environment)
nodes.rationale: Hermetic, version-pinned and the better default where Docker exists — this ADR says it should be revisited there. It simply cannot run here: the suite would fail at fixture start.

nodes.label: PostgresFixture
nodes.rationale: Owns the connection string (overridable via BANKLAB_TEST_DB) and applies migrations once per run in InitializeAsync; shared through an xUnit collection so migrations run once rather than per test class.

nodes.label: Three isolation levers for shared-database tests
nodes.rationale: Unique data per test (what this repo does), a transaction rolled back per test, or a full Respawn reset. The middle one is the trap: it is the standard trick and silently does not work for code that manages its own transactions — exactly the pessimistic slice.

nodes.label: ADR-0016 Three-tier test strategy for concurrent code
Tier 1 — deterministic forced-interleaving tests
nodes.rationale: May assert a specific interleaving and its exact consequence, because timing is fully controlled. Risk: such tests rot into documentation — a test asserting a bug happens fails confusingly if someone fixes the naive handler, unless the name and comment make the intent obvious.

nodes.label: Tier 2 — invariant / chaos tests
nodes.rationale: Free-running, so it may assert only properties that hold under every interleaving: money conserved, balance never negative, no approved withdrawal silently erased. Coverage is probabilistic — 32 actors a handful of times explores a vanishing fraction of interleavings; it raises confidence, it does not prove absence of bugs.

nodes.label: Tier 3 — integration tests against real PostgreSQL
nodes.rationale: Concurrency tokens and row locks are database behaviour; mocking them means testing the mock. Costs an external prerequisite.

nodes.label: Never assert an ordering you did not force
nodes.rationale: Winners.Count.ShouldBe(1) is legitimate — 100 funds exactly one 100 withdrawal under any interleaving. winners[0].ActorId.ShouldBe("actor-3") is asserting the scheduler's mood and will fail eventually. This is the rule that keeps tier 2 honest.

nodes.label: Timing assertions must be relative, never absolute
nodes.rationale: Derived from a real M5 flake: two performance-ratio tests passed consistently, then failed under CPU saturation. The fix was deletion, not a wider threshold — a wall-clock ratio on contended shared hardware is a property of the machine, not the code, and performance claims belong to BenchmarkDotNet. whenAll < sequential / 2 survives a uniformly slower machine; whenAll < 400ms does not. Absolute lower bounds derived from the work itself are fine.

nodes.label: TimingSensitiveCollection
nodes.rationale: xUnit runs collections in parallel by default, so a test measuring 'is this faster?' was competing with three other tests for the same four cores — measuring the test runner rather than the code. The collection disables parallelisation for classes whose assertions involve elapsed time.

nodes.label: Vacuous test failure mode
nodes.rationale: An assertion so weak it can never fail — 'no exception was thrown' — while the code silently corrupts data. The naive withdrawal passes that test perfectly while destroying 400. A concurrency suite that has never gone red against known-broken code is unproven.

nodes.label: Shared invariants inherited via IWithdrawStrategy
nodes.rationale: The invariants are stated once and reused across every strategy, so a new strategy inherits the whole suite by implementing the interface. TheRaceIsDeterministic_SoTheTestIsNotFlaky runs the same forced interleaving 25 times — a test about the test infrastructure, guarding the property everything else depends on.

nodes.label: Where mutable state lives
nodes.rationale: Almost every concurrency question in the repo reduces to this. Red boxes (InMemoryAccountStore, SemaphoreSlim per account) are per process; green (PostgreSQL) is shared by every instance. Scale to three instances and the red boxes are duplicated three times — three separate stores, three sets of locks, coordinating nothing.

nodes.label: Three replicas behind nginx topology
nodes.rationale: Nothing about the code changed between the one-instance and three-replica diagrams. What changed is that `lock` now guards one third of the traffic, which is the same as guarding none of it. The database slices are unaffected because their coordination point was never in process memory.

nodes.label: A contended withdrawal, four ways
nodes.rationale: Naive loses an update because the gap between read and write leaves a stale value; the in-process lock is correct only because both actors share one semaphore object in one process; optimistic has nobody wait but the loser redo work; pessimistic has nobody waste work but the loser wait, and is a throughput disaster if the transaction is long.

nodes.label: Request path through a slice
nodes.rationale: HTTP → Endpoint.cs → Handler.cs → IInterleaveGate / store or DbContext / IContentionRecorder → SignalR hub → Angular timeline. Two files per slice, no dispatcher and no pipeline in between.

nodes.label: "Breaks down when…" column
nodes.rationale: The column that matters: senior interviews are mostly about knowing the limits of your own choices, and anyone can recite what they picked.

nodes.label: Scaling by layer (code, instances, data)
nodes.rationale: Layer 1 code: async all the way down, don't lock the hot path — one .Result anywhere measured 979 → 35 RPS, p99 105 ms → 3531 ms on identical hardware. Layer 2 instances: stateless services behind a load balancer, broken by anything in process memory including SignalR groups. Layer 3 data: shard hot rows, queue writes, read replicas, idempotency — one hot row serialises regardless of replica count, and replicas triple DB load.

nodes.label: The five sentences worth memorising
nodes.rationale: 1) A race condition is the gap between read and write, not simultaneity. 2) async is for waiting, Parallel is for working, Task.Run is neither. 3) Optimistic pays in wasted work, pessimistic pays in waiting, contention decides. 4) How you aggregate matters more than whether you parallelise. 5) Kubernetes multiplies instances; it doesn't make un-scalable code scalable.

nodes.label: Idempotency key
nodes.rationale: Gains: retries stop duplicating money. Costs: a key per operation, storage, an expiry policy. Breaks down when the client doesn't send a stable key — without one, 5 retries charged 5×.

nodes.label: One atomic statement (SET balance = balance - n WHERE …)
nodes.rationale: No coordination needed at all, but only works if the logic fits in one statement — it breaks down when your decision needs data the statement cannot see.

nodes.label: Throttled fan-out vs unbounded Task.WhenAll
nodes.rationale: Task.WhenAll: 2005 ms → 204 ms on 5 threads, but unbounded fan-out means with 10,000 items you are your dependency's outage. Throttling with SemaphoreSlim protects the dependency and is slower on purpose (603 ms vs 204 ms); it breaks down when Release() isn't in a finally and the pool shrinks to nothing.

nodes.label: ValueTask on hot sync paths
nodes.rationale: Zero allocation versus 720 KB, but it can only be awaited once — await it twice or store it and it is worse than Task.

nodes.label: Parallel + thread-local sums (964.6 μs, 0.28× sequential)
nodes.rationale: Measured on 100,000 accounts: 3.68× faster than the 3,447.0 μs sequential baseline, versus 38,212.4 μs (11.09×) for a lock per item, 9,375.4 μs (2.72×) for Interlocked per item and 35,704.9 μs for ConcurrentQueue. Aggregation strategy dominates the decision to parallelise.

nodes.label: Task.Run wrapping sync work — 1,857× slower
nodes.rationale: 11,121.993 μs against a 6.000 μs synchronous call, allocating 1,360,216 B. async Task always-completed costs 21.43× and 720,072 B; async ValueTask costs 2.16× and allocates nothing.

nodes.label: Uncontended cost of each synchronisation primitive
nodes.rationale: Against a 352.8 μs unsynchronised baseline: Interlocked.Increment 13.66×, lock 54.61×, ReaderWriterLockSlim (write) 59.23×, SemaphoreSlim.Wait 117.31×. Ordering the primitives by cost is the point, not the absolute numbers.

nodes.label: ShortRun / shared-VM measurement caveat
nodes.rationale: Produced on a 4-core shared cloud VM under a ShortRun job, so some Error values are the same order as the Mean. Fine for order-of-magnitude claims (11×, 1,857×), not fine for anything subtler — two results within 2× should be treated as about the same. Stated explicitly because a benchmark you can't state the conditions for is a number, not evidence.

nodes.label: Concurrency vs parallelism (one teller vs many tellers)
nodes.rationale: Concurrency is about structure — one teller, many customers in progress, which is async/await needing no extra cores. Parallelism is about execution — four tellers at four counters, which is Parallel.ForEach and PLINQ and needs cores, because a core is a teller. Either can exist without the other.

nodes.label: async is for waiting; Parallel is for working
nodes.rationale: For I/O the CPU has nothing to do while it waits, so parallelising just means more idle threads. For CPU work the CPU is the bottleneck, so async overlaps nothing. The single most common misunderstanding in .NET interviews.

nodes.label: Task.Run is not async
nodes.rationale: It moves synchronous, blocking work onto a thread-pool thread and then waits for it — on a web server usually worse than doing nothing, because two threads are consumed instead of one. async all the way down means the library genuinely releases the thread.

nodes.label: Race condition = read → think → write with an intervening write
nodes.rationale: Defining it as 'two things happening at the same time' is wrong and sends you looking for the wrong fix. Nothing has to be simultaneous — on a single core one thread need only be interrupted between the read and the write. The bug is the gap, not the check, which is why more cores, async, or a ConcurrentDictionary never fix it.

nodes.label: The three fixes: block, detect, or remove the gap
nodes.rationale: Stop anyone else writing during the gap (pessimistic locking), detect that someone did and start over (optimistic versioning), or remove the gap by making read-decide-write one atomic operation.

nodes.label: Optimistic (apologise later) vs pessimistic (ask permission first)
nodes.rationale: Optimistic assumes collisions are rare and pays in wasted work, failing badly under high contention; pessimistic assumes they are common and pays in waiting, failing badly when transactions are long. Neither is better — the deciding variable is how often two people actually collide, and the trap is that both look fine in testing where you are the only user.

nodes.label: Concurrent collections protect their invariants, never yours
nodes.rationale: ConcurrentDictionary is thread-safe and does not save you: TryGetValue, decide, TryUpdate is still a race. A comment saying exactly this lives in InMemoryAccountStore.

nodes.label: Lesson 01 — Race conditions: who wins, and who loses silently
The lost update (measured: -400 discrepancy)
nodes.rationale: Five actors withdrawing 100 each from a 100 balance are all approved; the balance reads 0 while 500 left the bank. Every line of the naive read-think-write is defensible — no null check missing, no off-by-one — which is why reviewers approve it.

nodes.label: Silent losers
nodes.rationale: Unlike an ordinary bug, the symptom is a success response: nothing throws, nothing logs, every customer gets 200 OK. Found by an auditor months later rather than by tests. Detection in production needs invariants — a reconciliation job asserting the sum of transactions equals the balance delta; if you can't state your invariant you can't detect its violation.

nodes.label: The sawVer column — every actor read version 1
nodes.rationale: The whole bug in one column of the recorded timeline: three actors each computed 100 - 40 = 60 from the same stale snapshot and each wrote 60. The final version descends from version 1, so the intervening versions and the withdrawals they represented were erased with no error anywhere.

nodes.label: RunSummaryCalculator
nodes.rationale: Decides who won by replaying writes against the version each actor read, not by comparing balances (two actors can write the same value). Works unchanged for the in-memory counter and for Postgres xmin, because it only needs versions to be unique, never ordered.

nodes.label: forceRace parameter
nodes.rationale: Makes the interleaving a parameter instead of an accident: gate.ReachAsync at InterleaveCheckpoints.AfterRead is a no-op dictionary lookup in production and a barrier in a forced run, so the lost update happens 100% of the time and a test asserts it across 25 consecutive runs. A test that catches a bug one run in twenty is a flaky test, and flaky tests get muted.

nodes.label: Why tests don't catch it — the test is the only user
nodes.rationale: WithoutContention_TheNaiveVersionIsPerfectlyCorrect passes, and so does the integration test and QA, because the bug needs a second actor to arrive during the gap and in testing there is rarely a second actor.

nodes.label: The naive handler is correct for a single writer
nodes.rationale: Simplest and fastest — no locks, no retries, no round-trips — and genuinely right where an account is only ever written by one process in one place, such as a single-consumer queue. What makes it unacceptable for money is that it fails silently, and silent corruption is worse than a crash.

hyperedges.label: Process-local state that silently stops working at N replicas
The machinery that makes a race reproduce 100% of the time
Blocked CDN, no Docker daemon, no proxy egress — constraints that decided three ADRs
